posts.title: Eighth Update: Poland and Fort Worth
posts.author: George Parker Young
posts.excerpt: Home for Father's Day after two intense weeks on the Poland–Ukraine border — the incoming team, a story on myself at the train station, and a reading list on tyranny from Applebaum and Snyder.
posts.body:
Greetings friends and family. Happy Father's Day! I have been home in Fort Worth for almost three weeks, and been catching up in person with family and numerous friends, including trips to Waco to meet in person with Unbound Now leadership and to stay with music-playing friends, and to Lufkin for a majestic, inspiring memorial service for a close friend's mom.

I have a confirmed return to Poland in mid-August for at least five weeks, perhaps longer, with stays in at least a couple of adjoining countries, with some of that depending on how Putin's war is proceeding. So, once I get this Update out, you will not receive another update from me until late August, and that from Poland.

## Last Two Weeks in Poland

Though it seems ages ago, the last two weeks in Poland were very busy and productive, though varied in tasks and cities. That stint continued in Warsaw, working on lawyer follow-up aimed at getting the Unbound Now Europe non-profit foundation set up, meetings with Allison and other NGO leaders, and preparing logistics for the next team. Then to Krakow to meet the next incoming team of six. The day before the next team's arrival, I had a lovely long lunch with Alex, Sam and Talia off of the main Krakow Old Town Square. Though it had only been about a month since I had seen Talia, she had grown a bunch and was even more alert, engaging and active. She will be driving and sneaking out of the house at 8-9 months, is my best guess, assuming she has started walking by the end of this month. Alex and Sam were figuring out their best opportunity for service over the coming months, and whatever they decide that corner of the world will be so much brighter.

The next day I picked up most of the new incoming team in shifts at the airport, then our first evening meal and their orientation of several days in Krakow commenced, with their first trip to the border planned for later in the week. Arriving in Krakow the next day was Noah, and the Unbound Now Executive Director from Houston, Kerri, along with Allison, after they had done some incredible work with a Ukrainian church, refugee center and orphanage in Warsaw setting a foundation for the team's later work. Kerri has done incredible things for Unbound Now in Houston, not only implementing a dynamic victim recovery program but training literally thousands of professionals — teachers, health care workers, law enforcement — in human trafficking prevention education and Unbound Now's mission. I was privileged to watch a couple of her training sessions of the new team, which was some of the best teaching I have ever seen.

The geographic origins of this group of team members were very diverse: Megan in DC; Ashley in Fort Collins, Colorado; Cole in DC, who took all of his annual two weeks' vacation as an engineer with the DOD to perform his service in Poland and Ukraine; Bella in Waco; and Noah in Duke Divinity School. Noah has a specialization in the Catholic schism that resulted in the Orthodox church, so he was a great guide to the churches and history in Poland and Ukraine back to before the Crusades. Megan was a very strong team leader, who I never saw in anything but an ebullient mood. Ashley is finishing school and planning her next few years of service. Bella is another quiet one never to be under-estimated, with zingers for yours truly at just the perfect moments. All have been across the world on other mission trips, and each had some frightening stories of foreign reactions to their groups' work in countries that ban, and punish, anyone spreading Christianity.

The team's schedule called for two days on the border, one at the train station in Przemysl and the other in Medyka across into Ukraine. Of all the stories I could include on the team's work, please allow me to tell one on myself, and Kerri at the train station, where the flow was still steady, but now mostly back into Ukraine. One of the Ukrainian refugees we encountered was determined to get to London, and Kerri took her under her wing and spent more than an hour trying to help her, made more complicated by being consigned to Google Translate to overcome the language barrier. At one point it became clear this refugee needed to get to the local refugee center. I had no luck getting past the transport window, since the lady there insisted that no one could go to the refugee center without a ticket to their next destination, which our refugee did not have. But Kerri refused to accept my explanation of this interaction with authority, and next spent 15 minutes befriending that same window lady to the point that she herself drove our refugee to the refugee center, train ticket or not! And that is how very effective Kerri is, and sometimes we lawyers, who accept the official position, are not.

The team also put up new Unbound Now posters warning of trafficking risks in every business around the train station, with owner consent, and handed out new two-sided cards in the station — these now have a QR code for information on safe transportation, lodging, and other resources for refugees, all in Ukrainian and Polish.

## Why Ukrainian Refugees and Not Other Refugee Crises?

There is one issue I have put off discussing for several updates, that I would now like to take head on. The issue, as worded by a devil's advocate: why are you responding so viscerally to this Ukrainian humanitarian refugee crisis, George, and not earlier to other recent ones? After a lot of reflection and prayer, I personally must plead to being perhaps somewhat guilty, though there are a few mitigating circumstances I would join with my plea.

Here I would draw a bright-line demarcation between yours truly and Unbound Now. Unbound Now has responded strongly to many of the recent refugee crises, including Syrian, African, and others. It has offices in Mongolia and Indonesia and other foreign countries, with neither ethnic prejudice nor bias in the least. Unbound Now responds where the human trafficking problem is most acute. Anywhere in the world.

As for me, comparing this refugee crisis to others of the past decade seems to be measuring suffering in a way that is somewhat callow. Recent articles put the number of currently displaced humans at 100 million worldwide. The Ukrainians are protagonists in a war they neither incited nor invited, against a truly craven, unprovoked invasion, with Ukraine led by a once-every-hundred-years leader. For our generation, this is the first European land war in our lifetime. Given my long study of European history, for me this made doing something mandatory. And now that I am better-educated on the scope and victims of human trafficking, I am fairly hopeful I will be drawn to address the problem elsewhere in the future.

## A Crash Course from Anne Applebaum and Tim Snyder

For a short, more general sample of the problem with brief overviews of recent European history, I highly recommend Anne Applebaum's Twilight of Democracy. It takes two days to read, at most. Even shorter and more concise, I recommend Tim Snyder's On Tyranny. Then I have circled back with Applebaum's Red Famine: Stalin's War on Ukraine, and I am now halfway through her Iron Curtain: The Crushing of Eastern Europe.

Applebaum combines exquisite scholarship with personal interviews and elegant writing. A few highlights from Red Famine: the short-lived Ukrainian national movement between 1917 and 1933; the Holodomor, the Russian starving of Ukraine along with the murder and repression of Ukrainian intellectuals, professors, artists and writers; the earlier confiscation of grain by Russia from Ukraine beginning in 1917; and that both Lenin and Stalin saw Ukraine as a place to be looted to feed Moscow. The word Ukraine translates to border, even though it lacks natural borders. I will end with words Applebaum quotes from Voltaire: Ukraine has always aspired to be free.

Thanks so much, George

posts.title: Seventh Update: Krakow
posts.author: George Parker Young
posts.excerpt: Written in the shadow of Uvalde and Buffalo — a short, heavy dispatch before heading home to Fort Worth.
posts.body:
Uvalde, Texas. And Buffalo, New York. "Jesus Wept." John 11:35. "Then was fulfilled what was spoken by the prophet Jeremiah… Rachel weeping for her children; she refused to be consoled, because they were no more." Matt. 2:18.

I head home to Fort Worth tomorrow, and this will be the last Update for a couple of weeks — the above was the best I could do for this Seventh Update. My current plan is to return to Poland before June 21. I will write of the last two weeks and the down time and return when next I send an Update.

Please take care and hug every loved one near to you.

— George

posts.title: Sixth Update: Warsaw and Krakow
posts.author: George Parker Young
posts.excerpt: Field notes on the food, culture and vibe of Warsaw and Krakow — the Vistula, zurek soup, cigar-lounge conversations, and a housing boom reshaping the countryside.
posts.body:
I promised to write a little about the food, culture and vibe in Warsaw and Krakow. First of all, these are two beautiful, historic European cities. Warsaw is largely re-built after the destruction of World War II, though it has an old-European feel in many parts, along with a very modern skyscraper-filled downtown. Krakow was spared destruction and has castles and churches dating back to the 12th century, or earlier.

Dominating the country much like the Mississippi River does the US, the Vistula connects the three main cities, running from the Carpathians south to north into the Baltic Sea — Krakow to Warsaw to Gdansk. In Warsaw there is a gorgeous Calatrava bridge over the Vistula, translated as Holy Cross Bridge, and it rivals his Woman's Bridge in Buenos Aires. The Vistula appears in written records from the 1st century AD, including the writings of Pliny the Elder and Ptolemy.

The food in the two cities is first rate. The restaurants are fantastic and very reasonable. Three blocks from my Warsaw apartment is a restaurant that serves the best lobster bisque, with a diminutive spoon of black Polish caviar on the side. My cheap studio apartment is right off the main pedestrian walkway in Stare Miasto (Old Town), and so sitting at a coffee shop writing these updates and watching so many nationalities walk by has been very pleasant. All of the ubiquitous planters on this boulevard are in Ukrainian colors.

My go-to in many restaurants is the native Polish soup called Zurek. It is a sour rye, fermented, broth-based soup with interesting spicing and white kielbasa sausage and at least one divided boiled egg. It is nourishing and fortifying. If in doubt, I order the Zurek. But I have for the most part avoided the borscht — except at one very good restaurant in Krakow, Farina, where I had the best pickled beet salad with goat cheese mousse I could ever imagine.

In both cities there are wonderful cigar lounges, so I have not been deprived of my weekly smoke. I have met some very interesting characters in these shops, from contractors headed to or returning from Ukraine, to a German birthday vacationer, to a Brit with a Polish girlfriend whose grandfather survived WWII. Something about a relaxed cigar smoke and folks will chat. One thing that drives me a bit nuts is that in all coffee shops and restaurants they play almost exclusively American music — good American music, but it gives even the most authentic place an otherwise unmerited tourist feel. At the coffee shop next to my apartment, as I ordered my late-night decaf mocha, the Eagles' "Take It Easy" came on, and I'd had enough: I broke out into full-voiced sing-along, to the bemusement and delight of those in line. A man's got to sing what a man's got to sing.

The Polish are highly educated, a seemingly happy people as a group, comfortable with their place in the world and economically thriving. And clearly, they did not hesitate to step up on the Ukrainian refugees as no country has in a refugee crisis in a century. While I still struggle to pick up Polish vocabulary, there is a lilt, a positive uplifting note in almost every conversation I overhear. Everyone has been between exceedingly polite, to warm and welcoming.

There is a housing construction boom underway in Poland, mostly in the outlying villages and suburbs — unprecedented since the early 70s. For decades houses were built without incurring debt, so construction would take years. But now there is loan capital widely available. The average mortgage is under $500 a month. Almost 1.7 million new homes have been built in Poland in the last decade, and this new construction is everywhere one goes.

It is difficult for an outsider like yours truly to determine exactly how much the events of WWII still shadow the Polish; there is very little vestige of the communist era, except the almost universal loathing of the Russian leadership. In Warsaw there is a recently finished museum in remembrance of the Jewish ghetto that existed between 1940 and 1943 (for an excellent article on the historical ambiguity around Polish memory, see The Atlantic, February 2018). One detail from German Nazi propaganda circulated in the ghetto before its destruction: join a work detail and there will be food and shelter. This is hauntingly similar to the offers criminal traffickers are currently circulating to displaced Ukrainians.

Poland was the first to recognize the break-away Republic of Ukraine as the Soviet Union disintegrated, and pretty quickly the two signed mutual support treaties and declared there was no territorial dispute between them. We are all the beneficiaries of now thirty years of serious efforts at creating peace between these two peoples. Shortly after the Germans invaded Poland in 1939, an overly optimistic radio broadcast closed with the declaration: Long Live Poland! This became a rallying cry in the ghetto, the resistance, and later in the 70s and 80s.

So I close with this: Long Live Poland! And Long Live Ukraine. Again, thanks for all the good thoughts, prayers and notes of encouragement. Means so much.

George

posts.title: Fifth Update: Warsaw, Krakow and Warsaw
posts.author: George Parker Young
posts.excerpt: A week chartering Unbound Europe as a Polish foundation, and a Goya Foods press conference in Krakow on the trafficking risks facing Ukrainian refugees.
posts.body:
Good afternoon from Warsaw. This week included a good series of meetings with Allison, Jessica and the Polish lawyer in Warsaw working on obtaining Unbound Europe its charter as a Polish government-recognized foundation, from which EU NGO status flows. I also had the privilege of representing Unbound at a press conference Thursday in Krakow conducted by Goya Foods' CEO, alongside several of Goya's partners in its relief efforts here in Poland and Ukraine. The week also started with my introduction to the next arriving Unbound team, and while I did not think any group could match the last team, it appears this one will.

Monday was spent meeting with Allison and Jessica, Unbound's Development Director, and then with the wonderful Polish lawyer my former law partner Karen referred us to. As the Project Director for Unbound's efforts in Europe, Allison's preparation was essential. Lawyer Patrick had sent us a list of documents and issues to cover, and Allison, along with Stephanie of Unbound Waco and Fort Worth — a strong lawyer in her own right and also Allison's mom — worked up good written responses. Allison and Patrick largely conducted the meeting, and I should say again how impressive Allison is. I have seen ten- to twenty-five-year lawyers run such a meeting into a ditch, and this second-year law student handled it with preparation, poise and aplomb. This process takes about six months, and is far more complicated than chartering a Texas non-profit, in large part because Polish foundation law is very exacting and the EU recognition that comes with Polish foundation status is well worth the effort.

I dare say Allison will now be able to ace her second-year A&M Law Entities final exam before the first class is over, with the added special claim of having overseen the formation of a Polish and European NGO entity — something I might wager even the professor has never done.

The last third of our meeting with Patrick was spent hearing his particular take on the Ukraine refugee crisis. He called phase 1 the heroic phase, and that is now transitioning to phase 2, when the tasks will become much more difficult and complicated. He spoke eloquently about what his circle of friends is doing to address the situation — seemingly everyone he knew in Poland was doing something significant to help.

Tuesday and Wednesday I took the train from Warsaw to Krakow for the press conference. Please allow me to confirm how totally civilized the Polish train experience is: tickets purchased online, clean well-lit stations, clear signage, spacious seats. Three hours down to Krakow, almost four back, all for about $32 US.

Goya Foods is a good collaborator with the Houston Unbound office, and I was there — in a non-speaking role — mainly to show that Unbound was supporting the Goya efforts, and to deliver samples of our new anti-trafficking cards that Goya and its partners had tentatively agreed to distribute with relief supplies. Goya has already donated over 1 million pounds of food to the Ukraine relief efforts. And I should say the Goya Foods CEO, Bob Unanue, and I could not disagree more on matters political. But that is the great thing about the human trafficking problem: it crosses all political and philosophical lines as to the right thing to do. As a touching handwritten note to Barbara Jordan said, which I paraphrase from memory: you are Black, I am White; you are from the South, I am from New England; you are a Democrat and I am a lifelong Republican; but let me just say how much this Yankee appreciates your expression of good old Texas common sense the other night. That is the way I felt after Bob Unanue and the four other Goya partners had delivered their remarks.

Before I describe the other speakers, let me remind you of numbers each of you has already seen this week: 14 million Ukrainians displaced by Putin's war; 6 million fleeing the country with an estimated 1 to 2 million returning so far; more than 3,500 civilians killed. Poland has taken in over 3.2 million refugees, with Romania taking more than 900,000. And now this chilling number: searches for Ukrainian escorts in the UK have increased by over 660% — the traffickers are no doubt creating demand by exploiting the most disadvantaged.

The press conference was at the Sanctuary of Divine Mercy, a modern and impressive Roman Catholic basilica. Sister Teresa de la Fuente was a very impressive public speaker whose remarks worked in the themes of divine mercy and the best way to answer evil. Michael Caponi from Global Empowerment Mission kept it short, but they are making huge relief efforts here. Szymon Czyszek was the most impressive speaker — Polish, a lawyer, and in charge of the Knights of Columbus development efforts in Europe, which have a long-term presence here and are working on phase 2 and 3 problems including jobs, partnering with Indeed. The last speaker was with Aerial Rescue, ex-military volunteers focused on getting orphans and other vulnerable Ukrainians out of war zones; his view is that human trafficking is a greater black market, dollar-wise, than drugs and arms sales.

Thankfully, no media-speaking role for me, but I met all the main players after and they seemed very pleased someone from Unbound was there. The new Unbound cards for distribution were well received. So overall well worth the trip. Following up with those contacts was my main Friday project.

On the home front, Robert and Kathy are in Colorado visiting Caroline, who is completing her second half-marathon today. I miss home terribly, and this is the longest Kathy and I have been apart since we met in 1989. My current plan is to come home for a couple of weeks in early June, then to return to Poland for a month. Thanks again for all of the encouraging texts, emails and prayers.

With gratitude, George
